0: This is a real and painful lesson.
1: When I was doing model training for a business team, I assumed that a newer model with better scores on general leaderboards would perform better in the business scenario.
2: When a model with outstanding results on general leaderboards came out, I confidently promised that a better fine-tuned model would be ready straight away.
3: But that is not how it works, because every model uses very different data in pre-training and post-training. Some happen to have seen a lot of data similar to your business during pre-training, so fine-tuning gets twice the result for half the effort; others are strong in general but “mismatched” with your domain, and no amount of tuning gets them over the line.
4: When selecting a model, general metrics can only be a reference; the final choice still depends on performance on your business data.
6: When choosing a model we often look first at leaderboards, download counts or reviews, or just prepare a few questions and ask the model to see how it answers. These methods give a quick impression of a model, but all have limits.
7: For example, a high download count does not necessarily mean the strongest model; it may relate to release date, parameter size and how hard it is to use. And answering a few questions well does not mean the model keeps the same quality across that whole category of questions.
8: Especially when choosing among several models: if each is tested with different questions, or judged by different standards, they are hard to compare directly. Sometimes two models both look good, but once you test them on hundreds or thousands of records, accuracy and stability can differ markedly.
9: The purpose of model evaluation is to turn loose evaluation standards into a more unified testing method. For example, prepare 500 fixed test questions, have candidate models such as Qwen and DeepSeek answer them, then compute accuracy with the same rules. That compares the overall quality of different models and reduces the influence of personal judgement on the result.
10: Through model evaluation you see not only the final score but also which tasks a model does better on, which kinds of questions it tends to get wrong, and how large the gap between models is. These results help you pick a more suitable model from several candidates and provide a reference for later business-data testing, fine-tuning and deployment.
12: To make models easier to compare, benchmarks contain different kinds of data, for example,
13: MMLU covers questions from many subjects such as maths, history, computer science and law, mainly to observe a model's knowledge and reasoning ability;
14: C-Eval and CMMLU contain many Chinese exam and knowledge questions, useful for testing a model's Chinese knowledge ability;
15: GSM8K consists mainly of maths word problems and can test mathematical reasoning;
16: HumanEval mainly tests a model's ability to write code to a requirement;
17: IFEval focuses on whether a model can complete a task while following the user's requirements.
18: For actual evaluation you can pick data closer to your own scenario according to your business needs. For example, if the scenario cares most about Chinese knowledge Q&A, focus on datasets involving Chinese understanding, knowledge and reasoning; if the model is mainly for mathematical reasoning, focus on maths datasets such as GSM8K.
19: These public benchmarks let you compare different models on the same data and shortlist some whose abilities fit the requirement.But a high benchmark score does not mean the model will necessarily work well in real business.
20: The data in public benchmarks is general data, while real business may contain a great deal of specialist terminology and internal rules that are hard to test with public datasets. In other words, benchmarks let you do a first screen and pick models that look good, but the performance in your specific scenario still needs testing with business data.
22: General benchmarks measure a model's general ability, while business evaluation focuses on its actual performance in a specific scenario. After the first screening round, the key question is clear: is this model actually suitable for our business?
23: Business-data evaluation is essentially using data produced by the real business to verify the model. For example: for smart customer service, use real user enquiry records; for an enterprise knowledge base, use employees' day-to-day searches and questions; for industrial operations, use frontline equipment fault logs.
24: When preparing evaluation data, people often assume more data is always better. Representativeness and coverage matter more than sheer quantity. If you prepare tens of thousands of records but most are simple, repetitive questions, even a high score has little reference value. A sensible business test set should have a clear gradient: everyday high-frequency basic questions, plus a proportion of complex long questions and edge/exception cases. Only layered real data gives objective results.
26: EvalScope is the large-model evaluation framework from the ModelScope community. It can evaluate and compare the quality and inference performance of different models in a unified way. EvalScope covers a wide range, including large language models, multimodal models and the embedding and reranker models common in retrieval. Its strengths are:
27: 1) Covers both general benchmarks and custom business evaluation
28: EvalScope ships with common public benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K and HumanEval, so you can evaluate a model's general knowledge, maths, code and logical reasoning directly. It also supports custom evaluation sets: bring real business data such as text classification, Q&A or information extraction into the evaluation flow to judge a model's performance in a concrete scenario accurately.
29: 2) Supports many ways of connecting models and calling services
30: EvalScope evaluates local offline models and is also compatible with standard OpenAI-format endpoints. Model services deployed with mainstream inference engines such as vLLM or SGLang can be evaluated directly, fitting different development and deployment environments.
32: Besides quality, the running performance after deployment is also important when choosing. EvalScope can simulate concurrent requests from many users and measure core metrics such as throughput, request latency, time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT), reflecting how a service handles concurrency and how quickly it responds.
33: 4) Provides multi-dimensional comparison and report visualisation
34: After evaluation, EvalScope generates statistical reports and comparison charts automatically.

63: Next, use EvalScope to evaluate performance. The metrics people usually care about are time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT).
65: --model qwen3.5-2b: the model name, which must match the model name configured in the vLLM inference service
66: --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions: the actual endpoint of the model service
67: --api-key sk-123456: the API key. Required if the server authenticates; it can be omitted if none is configured.
68: --dataset random: use randomly generated test data, so no local test file is needed.
69: --tokenizer-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B: the path or Hugging Face name of the tokenizer, used to control the token length of generated text precisely.
70: --min-prompt-length 1024 and --max-prompt-length 1024: control the input prompt length range. Setting both to 1024 fixes every request's input at 1024 tokens.
71: --min-tokens 1024 and --max-tokens 1024: control the output length range. Setting both to 1024 forces the model to output exactly 1024 tokens each time (ignoring the end token).
72: --parallel 1 2 4 8: set the concurrency steps. The stress test simulates 1, 2, 4 and 8 users sending requests at the same time, to observe behaviour under different concurrency.
73: --number 10 20 50 100: set the total requests at each concurrency step. The list corresponds one-to-one with --parallel: for example 10 requests at 1 concurrency and 100 at 8 concurrency.
